summary: Describes a process in which a working group chair or secretary acts as the Document Shepherd for a document from working group last call through publication. Previously the responsible Area Director usually played this role. The memo aims to improve and speed up IETF document flow. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A long paper needs someone to walk it through each step until it is printed. This note says the group's leader, instead of a busy boss, can be that guide.

questions: how does the ietf approve documents
subtitle: Delegating document oversight to the working group level speeds up IETF publication

tldr.problem: IETF documents go through a slow review process after working group approval because a single Area Director must oversee many documents and provide detailed feedback, creating a bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a process where a working group chair or secretary serves as the "Document Shepherd" for their group's documents, handling feedback coordination during area director review, IESG review, and post-publication work, while the Area Director focuses on higher-level decisions.
tldr.outcome: Documents move faster through the approval process because the shepherd knows the document deeply and can respond quickly to feedback, unburdening the Area Director to focus on strategic issues.

today: RFC 4858 is an informational document from May 2007 describing the Document Shepherding process. It has not been obsoleted. The process remains in use across the IETF as the standard way to coordinate document review from working group approval through publication.

sections.title: The Document Bottleneck
sections.content:
The IETF publishes technical standards (RFCs) following a process where a working group develops a document, the group votes to approve it (Working Group Last Call), and then the document enters the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) approval pipeline. The Area Director responsible for that working group evaluates the document and decides whether to approve it for publication.

Historically, the Area Director handled all follow-up coordination. When reviewers (including other Area Directors on the IESG) raised questions or issues with the document, the Area Director tracked them, communicated with document editors, gathered consensus from the working group, and ensured issues were resolved. Area Directors often oversee many working groups and dozens of concurrent documents, making this coordination slow and sometimes overlooking details.

The PROTO team (PROcess and TOols team) at the IESG recognized that this created a bottleneck. A document shepherd—someone intimately familiar with one document—could handle the detailed coordination faster than a busy Area Director juggling many documents. This RFC describes that process, tested in 2004 and adopted as the IETF standard by the end of that year.
sections.eli5: When an Area Director has a hundred documents to approve and only so much time, each document gets little attention. If you put someone from the working group in charge of just their few documents, they can answer questions faster and move things forward.

sections.title: What is a Document Shepherd?
sections.content:
The Document Shepherd is usually a working group chair or secretary who becomes the primary point of contact and coordinator for a single document from working group approval through publication. (Rarely, if both chairs are also the document's authors, the secretary may serve as shepherd to avoid conflicts.)

The shepherd is not responsible for technical content; the document authors and working group still own that. Instead, the shepherd is a process manager: they track feedback, communicate with reviewers and editors, ensure issues are understood and resolved, and keep the document moving forward.

The shepherd should not be a primary author or editor, so they can maintain objectivity when issues arise. The same person shepherds the entire lifecycle from working group approval through final publication, ensuring consistency and accountability.
sections.eli5: A document shepherd is like a project manager for one document. They are not writing it, but they make sure all the feedback gets answered and nothing falls through the cracks.

sections.title: The Shepherding Process
sections.content:
The shepherding process begins when the working group votes to approve a document for publication. The shepherd writes two pieces: the Shepherd Write-Up and the Document Announcement Write-Up.

The Shepherd Write-Up answers a ten-part questionnaire, describing the working group process that led to approval. It covers questions like: Is the shepherd confident this version is ready? Has it received adequate review? Are there known contentious issues? Does the document meet all formal checklists? Are the IANA sections clear? This document informs the Area Director of any concerns before detailed review even begins.

The Document Announcement Write-Up is a summary for eventual publication, covering the technical summary, working group consensus, document quality, and personnel involved.

As the document moves through Area Director (AD) evaluation, if issues arise, the AD sends them to the shepherd rather than directly to editors. The shepherd conveys these to editors and the working group, tracks responses, and validates that solutions address the concerns. This is typically faster than having the AD follow up, because the shepherd can read the AD's intention more quickly and keep stakeholders informed in real time.

When the document reaches IESG Evaluation (a vote by all Area Directors), the shepherd again coordinates responses to any DISCUSS (blocking) or COMMENT (informational) items raised by other ADs. The shepherd either negotiates a resolution with the raising AD or escalates to their own Area Director for escalation, keeping pressure on the document without letting issues languish.

After IESG approval, the shepherd continues coordinating with IANA (which may need to register new protocol codes) and the RFC Editor (who handles publication details), responding to requests and ensuring all pieces complete.
sections.eli5: The shepherd writes a summary of how the working group approved the document, then stays on the case as it passes through each review step. When someone raises a question, the shepherd explains it to the editors, waits for an answer, and reports back. This keeps things moving instead of waiting for a busy boss.

sections.title: Why Delegation Speeds Things Up
sections.content:
The key insight is asymmetry of focus. An Area Director oversees multiple working groups and dozens of concurrent documents. They review each document once, identify issues, and move on. If an editor is slow to respond or a question is misunderstood, the AD doesn't re-engage quickly; the document waits in a queue.

A Document Shepherd has one or two documents at a time. When an issue is raised, they immediately engage with the editors and working group to understand the request and track progress. They can clarify ambiguous feedback quickly with the raising AD, without going back to their own Area Director. This back-and-forth happens at shepherd speed, not AD speed.

Additionally, the shepherd brings technical and contextual knowledge. They know the working group's discussions, understand why certain design choices were made, and can identify when feedback misinterprets the document. They can suggest resolutions directly to editors instead of asking the AD to guess.

Finally, having a named shepherd creates accountability. Editors and reviewers know whom to contact; the process has no ambiguity. Issues are not forgotten because the shepherd tracks them and reports status.
sections.eli5: If one boss watches everything and an issue needs clarification, it sits in a queue until the boss has time. If someone close to the problem is authorized to get clarifications and move forward, things happen faster.

sections.title: When Not to Shepherd
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a few situations where shepherding is not appropriate. If the shepherd is also a primary author or editor of most of the working group's documents, conflict of interest makes the role problematic. If the Area Director expects communication difficulties with the potential shepherd—whether due to past tensions or documented concerns—forcing a shepherding relationship is counterproductive.

If the working group is very old, losing momentum, or winding down, introducing a new process may distract from completion rather than help. In these edge cases, the Area Director acts as shepherd using traditional procedures.

The RFC emphasizes that the Area Director retains discretion. Not every document or working group is right for shepherding, and the Area Director can decline to use the process if they foresee problems.
sections.eli5: Shepherding works best when the shepherd knows the document, is not deeply invested in the content, and has time to focus on it. If none of these are true, better to skip it and use the old way.
